title: Find All People With Secret
spaceBreakdown:
- vector<int> parent: n entries → O(n)
- vector<int> rnk: n entries → O(n)
- vector<bool> knows: n entries → O(n)
- unordered_set<int> involved: up to min(n, 2m) entries per group, temporary → O(n)
- unordered_set<int> knownRoots: up to min(n, 2m) entries per group, temporary → O(n)
- sort(): O(log m) stack (introsort)
- not counted: input meetings, returned vector
approach: Sort meetings by time and process them in time-grouped batches. For each batch of meetings sharing the same time, use Union-Find to connect all participants, then mark every person whose component contains someone who already knows the secret. After each time group, reset the DSU parent/rank for all involved people so stale edges from earlier times don't bleed into later groups. This correctly handles instantaneous same-time propagation while respecting temporal ordering across different times.
hints: If three meetings [1,2], [2,3], [3,4] all happen at time 5, and only person 1 knows the secret, how many people know it after time 5? What does that tell you about how to handle meetings that share the same time value?

Use Union-Find (DSU). Group meetings by equal time, union every pair in the group, then mark all members of any component that contains a secret-holder. In Example 3, at time 1 the meetings [1,2] and [2,3] are unioned into one component containing person 1 (who knows), so persons 2 and 3 both learn.

```
sort meetings by time
knows[0] = knows[firstPerson] = true
for each group of meetings with same time:
    union all pairs in group
    collect roots of involved people who already know
    mark every involved person whose root is in that set
    reset DSU parent/rank for all involved people
return all people with knows == true
```

**Stale DSU edges** - A person unioned at an earlier time stays linked when processing a later time group.
`Input: n=5, meetings=[[1,2,1],[0,1,2],[2,3,2]], firstPerson=4` → `Expected: [0,1,4]`
⚠️ Bug: not resetting DSU parent/rank after each time group → returns [0,1,2,3,4]

**Same-time ordering** - Multiple meetings at one time must propagate the secret through the whole connected group.
`Input: n=4, meetings=[[2,3,1],[1,2,1],[0,1,1]], firstPerson=1` → `Expected: [0,1,2,3]`
⚠️ Bug: processing same-time meetings one at a time in sorted order → returns [0,1]

**Disconnected components at same time** - Two separate meeting groups at the same time, only one connected to a secret-holder.
`Input: n=6, meetings=[[0,1,1],[2,3,1],[4,5,1]], firstPerson=1` → `Expected: [0,1]`
⚠️ Bug: marking all people involved at time 1 as knowing → returns [0,1,2,3,4,5]

**firstPerson absent from meetings** - The firstPerson may never attend any meeting.
`Input: n=3, meetings=[[0,1,1]], firstPerson=2` → `Expected: [0,1,2]`
⚠️ Bug: collecting only people who appear in meetings → returns [0,1]

followUps.q: What if meetings can also occur at time 0, competing with the initial sharing?
followUps.a: Process time-0 meetings after initializing knows[0] and knows[firstPerson]. The same group-by-time logic handles it since the initial sharing is instantaneous at time 0. TC and SC unchanged.

followUps.q: What if n can be up to 10^9 but only m meetings exist?
followUps.a: Replace the parent/rank/knows vectors with hash maps keyed on person ID. Only people appearing in meetings (plus 0 and firstPerson) need entries. TC stays O(m log m), SC drops to O(m).

followUps.q: What if a person who learns the secret can later forget it after a deadline?
followUps.a: The monotonicity assumption breaks. You would need a sweep over time tracking active knowledge intervals per person, merging intervals as meetings propagate. This becomes an interval-merge problem with TC O(m log m) but significantly more complex bookkeeping.
